Three Indian presidents received the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award, before they became president:

- **Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan**: awarded 1954, became president in 1962.
- **Zakir Husain**: awarded 1963, became president in 1967.

answer: Early Carboniferous, roughly 335–341 million years ago (Arthur's Seat, Edinburgh)
text:
[Historia Regum Britanniae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historia_Regum_Britanniae) is what made Arthur famous, but the name's origin is disputed, and [Arthur's Seat](https://storytellingdb.com/arthurs-seat-edinburgh/) notes a Camelot theory and a Gaelic-origin theory.
- The age is well supported. The [British Geological Survey's Earthwise entry](https://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/Arthur%E2%80%99s_Seat) describes it as an extinct volcano, with the exposed plug and vent system left as high ground after glaciers eroded the softer surroundings. The [Cockburn Association](https://www.cockburnassociation.org.uk/?p=6809) gives about 341 million years ago, and another guide gives about 335 million years ago.

I checked other candidates (Lear, Brutus, Lud, Bladud, Cymbeline, Leir, Gorboduc, Vortigern) and found no volcano named after any of them. Lear is a crater on Uranus's moon Oberon, not a volcano. Arthur's Seat is my best match, but I did not find a source that directly ties the name to the *Historia*.

HistoryLearning says the sides stayed on either side of the 38th Parallel through the first six months of 1951.
- **End:** The armistice was signed on July 27, 1953, at Panmunjom (per the Military Wiki and historycollection.com).

text:
The surname Sylvester comes from Latin, through the Latin name Silvester, which is based on *silvestris* ("wooded" or "wild") and *silva* ("forest"). The emperor crowned in 800 was Charlemagne. The Latin of his era is usually called Medieval Latin, also described as the language that developed from Late Latin between roughly the 4th and 10th centuries. Scholars disagree on exactly where Late Latin ends and Medieval Latin begins, and the label was applied retrospectively. The Carolingian court under Charlemagne is treated as a high point of this language rather than its origin.

The deepest point in the world's oceans is Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, southwest of Guam, at roughly 10,935 m (35,876 ft) by the search's figures. See [WorldAtlas](https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/what-is-the-deepest-part-of-the-ocean.html).
- **Richmond, Virginia (transit station):** This is the more likely reading, since the question implies a coastal state. Virginia borders the Atlantic, and the deepest known Atlantic point is Milwaukee Deep in the Puerto Rico Trench, at about 8,400 m (27,500 ft). This figure comes from my own knowledge, not the search results. Published values vary (roughly 8,376–8,605 m), so treat it as approximate.

**Persian Gulf (where Kharg Island is):** Sources disagree on the timing, depending on whether they mean the basin or the modern marine gulf:

- Another source says it has been formed around 15,000 years ago.
- A less specific claim is that about 500,000 years ago, the primitive form of the Persian Gulf was formed along the southern plains of Iran, and the Marine Insight page gives the same 500,000-year figure.
- Geologically, the basin is much older. One scientific source describes a tectonic basin of late Pliocene to Pleistocene age.

**Persian Gulf (where Kharg Island is):** Dates depend on whether you mean the basin or the modern sea:
- The modern gulf took its present form in the early Holocene, as sea level rose, roughly 12,000 to 6,000 years ago, per the [orchestrator's search results](https://www.marineinsight.com/know-more/persian-gulf-facts/). Another source in those results gives about 15,000 years ago.
- The tectonic basin is late Pliocene to Pleistocene in age, a few million years old, per the [Persian Gulf Basin entry](https://en.Wikipedia.com/wiki/Persian_Gulf_Basin). Sea level fell by as much as 120 m in the Pleistocene, draining the gulf at times.

I did not verify the 500,000-year figure for a primitive gulf, so I've left it out.
